newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's truth-seekers will not sniff out spies. [CORRECTED 15:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's truth-seekers will not sniff out spies. [CORRECTED 15:35 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects attribution from "John Allen, a spokesman" to "Alex Boraine, vice-chairman".)
South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission said on Thursday that it would not be manipulated into "sniffing out" informers who had once served the apartheid government.
"We are determined not to allow this issue to become a political football," Alex Boraine, vice-chairman of Nobel peace laureate Desmond Tutu's commission, said in a statement.

"It is also important to make it clear that the commission does not intend to launch a large-scale sniffing out of alleged informers. We have neither the resources, the time nor the inclination to do this," Boraine added.

Allegations surfaced recently during inquiries by the truth commission that up to five African National Congress (ANC) cabinet ministers spied on their own colleagues for the white regime during the war over apartheid.
The statutory truth commission's amnesty committee however initially ruled that spies identified during applications for immunity from prosecution for human rights crimes would not be publicly named.
But Tutu said last week it would be necessary to name the people implicated after giving them 21 days advance notice in order to halt the spread of lies and innuendo.
Boraine said the truth body, set up to probe 30 years of gross human rights abuses on all sides of the apartheid divide, wanted to act with caution in its investigations into specific charges.
"It is of critical importance that...it is kept in mind we are dealing with allegations which will need to be corroborated before any public announcement is made," he said.
A lawyer representing five apartheid agents seeking amnesty, Roelof du Plessis, earlier told the commission there are high-profile people in government who were informers.
Assassin Joe Mamasela, who has confessed publicly to several political murders, also said five ANC cabinet ministers had once worked for the apartheid police.
The outcome will be a test for the ANC, which has promoted open government and transparency in politics since it swept to power in the country's first all-race elections in 1994.
President Nelson Mandela and Deputy President Thabo Mbeki both favour the naming of alleged informers, with Mandela saying anyone whose actions led to deaths would be fired.
